answer_1.quote: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as transformative tools, with interactive systems being one of their most influential applications. From education to creative collaboration, LLMs are increasingly expected to engage in meaningful, multi-turn conversations that adapt to users with various needs and capabilities.
answer_1.outputs: multi-turn conversations in math tutoring and document creation

answer_2.quote: SimulatorArena enables automatic evaluation of (1) how closely simulator messages resemble real user messages, using metrics such as LLM-judged Turing tests, and (2) how well simulators align with human evaluations of assistants, measured by the correlation between the assistant ratings from the simulator and human users

answer_3.quote: To assess message similarity, we use two complementary evaluation methods with GPT-4o as judge: Likert Scale. We rate message similarity on a 1-5 Likert scale across two aspects: writing style and interaction style, with 5 indicating nearly indistinguishable from real user messages. Turing Test. We present two conversations to the evaluator, one between a real user and the AI, and one between a simulated user and the AI, and ask them to identify which involved the real user.

answer_4.quote: We use Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) to collect the human-LLM conversations, with 107 unique workers—66 for math tutoring and 75 for document creation—interacting with 9 LLMs.
answer_4.guideline: Users rate the assistant's interaction quality on a 1-10 scale. In math tutoring, they also submit a final solution; in document creation, they also provide a 1-10 rating for the final document. Additionally, users can give a thumbs up or down for each assistant response.
